linux: You are granting a reporting service access to /srv/reports/daily.csv, a regular file with mode 640. The service is not the file owner.
A Linux service runs under the app account. You need to adjust access to its configuration without changing the configuration contents or granting administrator privileges.
A deployment uses /srv/app/current as a symbolic link to a versioned release directory. Operators must understand what remains valid when old releases are removed.
A cleanup job encounters two filenames on the same filesystem that were created using ln without -s. You need to predict what deleting one name will do.
A shell script sends a diagnostic program's output through a parser using a plain pipe, with no explicit file-descriptor redirection.
A Bash maintenance script receives a filename in the variable file. Valid filenames can contain spaces and wildcard characters, and must be treated literally.
An operator records a service PID for a later maintenance action. The machine remains running overnight, and services may exit and start again before that action.
A worker buffers completed records in memory and needs a short cleanup interval when stopping. You are designing its normal shutdown procedure.
An application cannot write to /var, and you are comparing df with a directory-size scan. You need to understand which storage view each tool reports.
A spool directory stores millions of tiny messages. File creation starts failing even though the storage dashboard reports several gigabytes of unused capacity.
A server handles many simultaneous clients and opens a log file for each worker. You are investigating the operating-system limit reported as 'too many open files'.
A 16-core Linux host develops slow responses. Its load average rises, but CPU utilization alone does not explain the slowdown; storage behavior also needs investigation.
A monitoring alert uses the free column of a Linux memory report. Before escalating, you must determine whether the application actually lacks usable memory.
A containerized worker suddenly disappears after deployment. You have its exit status but have not yet established whether the cause was a memory limit or an external signal.
An HTTP service is expected to accept connections on TCP port 8080. Local tests and remote tests disagree, so you need evidence from the host's socket table.
An application and a command-line DNS client return different addresses for the same hostname on one Linux machine. You are comparing their lookup mechanisms.
A service cannot update files on a mounted data volume. You need to distinguish access rights from filesystem mount state before changing permissions.
A package upgrade has replaced a service executable on disk. The service has not been restarted, and an audit asks which code is currently executing.
A worker launches short-lived child processes. Monitoring shows many entries with state Z, and you need to identify the lifecycle responsibility involved.
An application stalls without useful error messages. You are considering strace on one affected process to identify the operating-system operations it is waiting for.
A batch job and an interactive API compete on the same Linux host. You are evaluating nice values as one control for their relative CPU access.
An API host develops latency spikes during peak traffic. Its memory workload has grown, and you are assessing swap activity before changing the host's memory policy.
A network service needs one privileged operation but otherwise performs ordinary application work. You are considering Linux capabilities as part of its deployment design.
A file uses a POSIX access control list with a named-user entry. The access shown for that entry differs from the effective access reported by getfacl.
Several processes read a configuration file while a deployment updates it. The update must avoid exposing a partially written file, and power-loss durability is a separate requirement.
Two containers on one Linux host see different process and network views. You are reviewing which isolation mechanisms apply and which resource controls are still needed.
A container's request latency rises under load even though the host has idle CPU cores. The service runs inside a cgroup with a configured CPU budget.
A production filesystem reports metadata errors. Applications are still writing, and the operator must choose a recovery approach that protects the remaining data.
A program measures request deadlines and also writes timestamped logs for other machines to correlate. The host's time synchronization service can adjust its calendar clock.
Several unrelated applications start reporting I/O failures after a host update. You are deciding whether to investigate their code independently or a shared operating-system layer.
networking: A client sends application records over a TCP connection. The receiver must parse records correctly even when reads return different byte counts than the sender's writes.
A sensor sends individual telemetry messages to a collector over UDP. You need to understand the transport contract before deciding whether to add acknowledgement logic.
A service is moving from an IPv4 endpoint to an IPv6-only endpoint. You are reviewing its DNS records and the address families supported by clients.
An operator changes a service's DNS address during a migration. Different clients observe the update at different times despite querying the same hostname.
Two Linux hosts are connected to the same Ethernet segment. Their IPv4 addresses and prefix lengths were configured manually, and direct communication is failing.
A host can communicate with a neighboring machine but cannot reach an address outside its local network. Several routes are installed, so route selection matters.
A host is trying to contact an IPv4 peer on the same subnet. You need to understand the neighbor-resolution step before traffic can leave the interface.
A server handles many clients on one TCP listening port. You are distinguishing a listening endpoint from the individual connections created for each client.
A client establishes a TCP connection to port 443, then fails before receiving an HTTP response. You must identify what the successful transport test actually proves.
An HTTPS client reaches a server and receives a certificate, but identity validation fails. Certificate trust and the requested DNS hostname must both be considered.
An HTTP request reaches a load balancer and receives status 503. You need to distinguish an application-layer response from a DNS or TCP connection failure.
Many private clients reach the Internet through one outbound translation device. New connection failures begin during a sharp increase in connection creation.
A request crosses a stateless subnet filter and a stateful firewall. Outbound traffic is allowed, but the reply never reaches the client.
An application works over a direct link but stalls for larger transfers after a tunnel is added. Small health-check requests still complete successfully.
A TCP application becomes slower during traffic bursts. You have request-duration data and retransmission counters, and need to relate them without assuming a cause prematurely.
A deployment creates a DNS record shortly after a client queried the name while it did not exist. Authoritative and recursive lookups now disagree.
A persistent TCP connection remains established while users receive no useful responses. The team is deciding whether transport keepalive is a sufficient health signal.
A client makes thousands of short HTTPS requests to the same service. You are investigating repeated connection and TLS setup as part of its latency budget.
Two HTTP applications share one public address and must receive requests according to URL paths. The routing layer must be chosen with the needed request visibility in mind.
A backend receives traffic both from a reverse proxy and from direct clients. An access rule uses a forwarded client-address header supplied in requests.
A dependency slows during peak traffic. Several callers retry at the same fixed interval, and the total request rate increases while useful completions fall.
A payment request crosses several services and eventually times out at the client. The client does not know whether the write completed before the response was lost.
A server receives incoming packets through one firewall, but its routing table sends replies through another path. The firewalls keep independent connection state.
A service advertises the same IP address from several geographic locations. A routing change shifts new traffic to another location while clients maintain ongoing sessions.
Traffic takes an unexpected upstream provider path even though another path has lower measured latency. You are reviewing BGP rather than application routing.
An IPv6 host stops communicating after a firewall update that rejects ICMPv6. Address configuration and local-neighbor communication must be checked separately from application ports.
A client repeatedly creates and closes TCP connections to one server. Its socket table contains many TIME_WAIT entries, and operators worry about available local ports.
Bulk transfers maintain good throughput while interactive requests become slow on the same link. You are examining the behavior of queues under sustained demand.
A reverse proxy terminates client HTTPS and opens a separate connection to the application. A security review covers both connection segments, not only the public endpoint.
An order-creation request may have succeeded even though its response was lost. The client needs a retry strategy that preserves the intended business effect.
sre: You support an online checkout service. Users report failed purchases while host CPU dashboards remain normal, and the team needs a measure of customer-visible behavior.
Product and operations teams need a shared definition of acceptable checkout reliability. They must decide how to evaluate performance over time rather than discuss individual outages alone.
A service has a documented reliability target and a release policy tied to it. Several recent releases caused failures, and the team is deciding whether to continue normal rollout activity.
During a customer-facing outage, several specialists join the response and begin proposing changes. The team needs clear decision ownership without preventing technical investigation.
A production release closely precedes a rise in failed requests. A tested rollback is available, but the exact code-level cause has not yet been established.
A recurring outage has already been discussed in an incident review. The next review must lead to changes that can actually be assigned, verified and followed through.
An operations team spends a growing part of every day repeating the same provisioning procedure. You are evaluating whether this work belongs in its toil-reduction programme.
A new on-call engineer must use an incident procedure under time pressure. The service has changed since the procedure was last exercised.
A service uses a 99.9% success SLO and burn-rate alerts. Responders need to distinguish short-lived noise from failures that threaten the available error budget.
An API's average response time remains stable, but some customers report multi-second delays. You must choose evidence that represents those users rather than only the average request.
The on-call rotation receives frequent overnight pages that rarely require intervention. The team is reviewing which conditions should interrupt a responder.
A service runs across several zones and must survive the loss of one. You are reviewing capacity during the failure, including traffic transferred to surviving instances.
An overloaded backend accepts requests faster than it completes them. Queue growth is increasing latency for both important and low-priority work.
A producer sends work to a queue consumed by a fixed worker pool. Arrival rate exceeds sustained processing rate, so the backlog continues to grow.
A request crosses three services, each with its own retry loop. You are examining how failure handling changes the number of attempts reaching the final dependency.
A backup dashboard reports successful jobs, but the team has never restored the current application version. A recovery exercise is being planned in an isolated environment.
A disaster plan promises service restoration within one hour. Recovery includes authentication, networking, data access and application startup, not just restoring a database.
A service's recovery agreement permits losing at most one hour of committed writes. You are checking whether its backup and replication design meets that requirement.
A team introduces a new API version to a small fraction of traffic. Some request categories behave differently, so overall error averages may not show the change clearly.
A newly enabled feature increases dependency load without changing the deployed binary. The team needs an operational control that can affect that behavior quickly.
Several otherwise unrelated services fail at the same time. All use a shared identity provider, and the response team is examining common failure paths.
An online store can accept orders without its recommendation component. You are designing behavior for a recommendation outage while preserving core customer journeys.
A team proposes deliberately disrupting a production dependency to test resilience. Before the experiment, you must define how it will be bounded and stopped.
An ongoing outage generates conflicting reports from support and engineering. Customers need reliable information even though the recovery time is not yet known.
One region has a severe customer-facing outage, but a global availability graph still meets target because most requests come from healthy regions.
A failed service has just restarted. Many clients reconnect at once while caches refill, and the recovering instances begin saturating again.
A network partition affects a service that updates account balances. The team must decide what operations remain available under its stated correctness requirements.
A reliability backlog contains frequent harmless alerts and a rare failure capable of affecting every customer. You need a basis for comparing engineering priorities.
A team reports improved average incident recovery time after changing severity labels. You must assess whether customer outcomes improved or the measurement population changed.
An automated remediation repeatedly restarts instances after a noisy signal. Some healthy instances are disrupted, so the team is reviewing the automation's decision boundaries.
systems: A Linux host uses systemd to supervise an API process. Operators see an active unit but must still determine whether the API is serving valid responses.
An administrator starts a service successfully during maintenance. The requirement is for it to return automatically after the next normal boot.
A packaged service needs a local resource setting that must survive package upgrades. The team wants to preserve the vendor unit while maintaining its customization.
An application failed to restart at 14:10 on a systemd host. You need relevant diagnostic records without searching unrelated services or the entire log history.
Several applications share a Linux server and currently run under one account. A security review asks how access to each application's private files can be separated.
A deployment system authenticates to production hosts using an SSH key pair. Its private key has appeared in logs accessible to a wider team.
A server depends on a system library installed outside the distribution's normal tooling. Operators need an inventory and a reliable security-update process.
A maintenance script runs successfully in an interactive shell but fails from a scheduled job on the same machine. You need to compare execution contexts.
Authentication errors and confusing log order appear across a fleet. One host's clock has drifted from the others, so time synchronization is part of the investigation.
Application data and system files share the root filesystem. Log growth causes service failures, and you are reviewing the storage layout for future operation.
A long-running application writes to a file rather than standard output. Operators rotate or remove the filename, but storage usage does not fall as expected.
A storage system has a continuously replicated second copy. An accidental deletion reaches both copies, and the team needs to recover an earlier valid state.
A database restore completes and the process starts successfully. Before declaring recovery, the team must determine whether the expected application data is actually usable.
A file server uses a redundant disk array. An operator accidentally deletes a project directory, and the team is evaluating what the array can recover by itself.
An administrator extends a logical volume supporting an application filesystem. The block-device capacity changes, but the application's filesystem report does not.
A machine has several attached disks and persistent mount entries. After a reboot, device enumeration differs from the order seen during installation.
A host stops reaching its normal boot target after an administrator changes mount configuration. Authorized recovery-console access is available.
A kernel security update has been installed on disk across a production fleet. The team must confirm that running hosts actually use the updated kernel.
An emergency fix changes a production host outside its declared configuration. The immediate incident is over, and the team is reviewing the long-term baseline.
A team member changes role or leaves the organization. You are checking administrative access, including credentials that may outlive the person's normal login.
A sudo rule permits a particular utility as root. The review must consider everything that utility can do, not merely the name of its primary function.
A service-specific limit was lowered during hardening. Under normal peak demand the service now fails, so you need to compare the limit with legitimate workload requirements.
Users see failed transactions even though CPU, memory and disk dashboards look healthy. You are reviewing whether monitoring covers the service as well as its host.
An engineer repairs one server manually, but new servers built from the approved image still fail. The fix must become repeatable across the fleet.
Storage demand grows steadily and capacity procurement takes several weeks. You must decide when to act, including room for recovery and failure scenarios.
A remote firewall update could interrupt the only SSH connection to a production machine. The change needs a recovery plan before it is applied.
A disk containing customer data is being retired. Removing its filesystem entries is not the only disposal step the organization needs to assess.
A kernel tuning change succeeds on a quiet test host. The production fleet includes heavily loaded databases with different behavior and availability requirements.
A disaster exercise assumes that the normal identity system is unavailable. Responders still need authorized access to instructions and recovery credentials.
An administration command exits successfully after reloading a service configuration. Customers continue seeing errors, so completion must be checked at the service boundary.
aws: A business plans recovery of an AWS-hosted application in a second geographic area. It needs to inventory which resources and dependencies must exist there.
An application runs in one AWS Region and must tolerate a zone-level failure. You are reviewing how compute placement and surviving capacity affect that goal.
An application needs to call AWS APIs from its runtime environment. The current image contains a static access key, and credential lifecycle is under review.
A workload's IAM policy permits actions on resources owned by other applications. You are reviewing permissions against the workload's actual operational requirements.
An application is being adapted to store data in S3. Its original implementation assumes local file operations and locking, so the storage interface must be reviewed.
An EC2-hosted database needs persistent block storage and a tested way to recover data. You are evaluating the role of EBS in that design.
An EC2 database should accept connections only from application servers. You are reviewing security-group rules and the sources those rules permit.
An EC2 instance is in a subnet described as public, yet outbound Internet access fails. You need to check what that label does and does not guarantee.
A private IPv4 workload needs to initiate connections to an external package service. It should not receive a directly reachable public address.
A workload in a private subnet needs to access S3. The design must work without depending on the proposed NAT path for that traffic.
An HTTP application is served through an Application Load Balancer. After deployment, requests fail and target health needs to be checked.
Queue workers wait on an external API, so CPU remains low while the age of pending work rises. You are choosing an Auto Scaling signal for this workload.
A CloudWatch dashboard combines measurements from several instances. One instance is unhealthy, but the combined graph appears normal.
A production resource was deleted through an AWS API. The investigation needs the responsible identity, time and operation rather than only application logs.
A public S3 access configuration exposes customer data. The team is deciding which security responsibilities belong to its own configuration and operating practices.
An application overwrites an S3 object with incorrect content. Bucket versioning was enabled before the change, and operators are investigating recovery options.
An RDS database experiences an availability failover. Application clients retain existing connections, and you need to assess behavior during reconnection.
An application sends writes to a primary database and some reads to a replica. A user reads immediately after updating a record and sees older data.
An event-driven Lambda function performs an order operation. The event source can deliver the same logical event more than once.
An SQS consumer processes work longer than expected. Another consumer receives the same message before the original worker finishes.
A queue contains a small set of messages that fail repeatedly. The team needs to isolate their failures without abandoning diagnosis or replay planning.
A DynamoDB table receives most traffic for a single customer identifier. Requests for that access pattern are throttled while other keys remain quiet.
A workload accesses an encrypted object and receives a decryption-related denial. Its identity permissions and the encryption key's authorization policy must be considered.
A database credential is rotated successfully in the secret store. Long-running clients continue using the old value and start failing authentication.
A Route 53 failover change directs the service name to a healthy endpoint. Some clients continue reaching the former endpoint for a while.
A CDN serves an application with both public and personalized responses. A user reports receiving content that belongs to someone else.
A CI pipeline in one AWS account must assume a deployment role in another. The operation fails despite the target role existing.
A demand spike triggers a scaling request, but AWS rejects creation of additional capacity. The team needs to distinguish quota limits from workload configuration.
A monthly AWS bill rises after several deployments. The investigation needs to connect usage with responsible applications and teams.
A disaster-recovery exercise starts the application in another Region but fails on supporting dependencies. The plan must be validated as a complete service recovery.
terraform: An operator changes a managed cloud resource manually during an incident. The versioned Terraform configuration is unchanged, and the next deployment is being prepared.
A CI runner checks out a Terraform project into a new working directory. It has not yet prepared the configured backend or installed provider dependencies.
A proposed infrastructure change includes a database that must retain its data. Before applying anything, the team needs to inspect the planned operations.
A cloud object exists, but Terraform does not associate it with the intended resource address. The team is investigating the relationship between configuration and remote objects.
A reusable module accepts an environment name from its caller. Invalid names should be rejected before they lead to confusing downstream resource failures.
A pipeline consumes values exported by a Terraform root module. Some outputs may contain credentials, so the output and logging behavior needs review.
A Terraform project is upgrading the plugin that manages its cloud resources. The proposed operations change even though the resource configuration looks the same.
Several teams maintain nearly identical infrastructure definitions with inconsistent defaults. You are evaluating how to share that configuration through a deliberate interface.
Two clean CI runners initialize the same Terraform configuration but select different provider builds. You are reviewing version constraints and the committed lock file.
Two engineers manage the same infrastructure using separate local state copies. They need a coordinated workflow that protects both state data and concurrent operations.
An interrupted CI job leaves a Terraform state lock behind. A new job cannot proceed, and the team must establish whether the original operation is still active.
A project marks a database password as sensitive. An engineer is deciding whether that makes its Terraform state file safe to publish.
A resource uses for_each with keys derived from a map. A refactor renames one key even though the team intends to preserve the same remote object.
A configuration creates several resources using count and a list of names. Removing the first list entry changes the plan for more resources than expected.
A resource has an operational prerequisite that is not represented by an attribute reference. The team needs Terraform's execution ordering to account for it.
A module needs an existing network's identifier, but a different team owns that network's lifecycle. You must choose how the module obtains the information.
A manually created database must become Terraform-managed without being recreated. Configuration, object identity and the resulting plan all need to be checked.
A refactor moves a resource into a child module. The desired cloud object is unchanged, but its Terraform address will differ.
A critical database resource has lifecycle protection in Terraform. Administrators also have direct cloud API access, so the protection boundary needs review.
A resource's lifecycle configuration ignores several attributes. One is security-related, and operators are reviewing which system should own changes to it.
A resource replacement is configured to create the new object first. The underlying service requires a globally unique fixed name and cannot host both objects with that name.
An operator uses -target for a narrow emergency Terraform change. The immediate operation succeeds, and the team needs to establish the remaining state of the full configuration.
A Terraform shell provisioner configures a host but fails partway through. The team is reviewing how to make configuration and recovery reproducible.
A team uses CLI workspaces for development and production. Both workspaces still use credentials capable of modifying production infrastructure.
A pipeline saves a Terraform plan for later approval and application. The artifact may contain evaluated values from configuration and state.
An incident response adds a firewall rule manually. Terraform later detects a difference, and the team must decide how that emergency change fits the intended baseline.
A small application change locks a large shared Terraform state containing unrelated infrastructure. Ownership, change frequency and failure scope are being reviewed.
A Terraform apply fails after some cloud operations have already completed. The team must determine the actual state before attempting recovery.
A major provider upgrade produces unexpected replacement actions for existing infrastructure. The team needs evidence before approving the upgrade.
A Terraform plan proposes exposing a sensitive service to the public Internet. A delivery policy is meant to identify unacceptable changes before application.
docker: An operator edits a file inside a running container to repair an application. The next deployment will create new containers, so the source of their filesystem must be understood.
A Docker build copies a credential into an image and removes it in a later instruction. The team is reviewing whether the resulting artifact is safe to distribute.
A CI job rebuilds an application from an unchanged Dockerfile. The base image uses a tag whose referenced content may have changed since the previous build.
A developer builds an image from a large project directory containing local credentials and unrelated files. The team needs to control which files the build can access.
A containerized API emits operational messages continuously. The host begins running out of disk space, and the team is reviewing collection and retention responsibilities.
An application listens on port 8080 inside a container. Clients connect through a host address, so both the container listener and published endpoint must be understood.
A database container will be replaced during deployment. Its data must remain recoverable independently of that container instance.
A container starts its service through a shell wrapper. During shutdown the application does not finish its normal cleanup, so process and signal behavior are being reviewed.
A containerized worker creates short-lived child processes. Operators observe unreaped children and need to understand the role of the main process.
A standalone Docker container remains running while its configured health check reports unhealthy. You need to distinguish that status from the response of a supervisor.
An application needs write access only to its own data directory. You are choosing its runtime identity without granting unnecessary host or container privileges.
A container terminates during a memory spike while the host still shows available RAM. It runs with an explicit memory limit.
An API container has a CPU quota and rising tail latency. The host is not fully busy, so container-specific scheduling constraints need investigation.
A container deployment mounts a host configuration directory. The same image behaves differently on two hosts whose filesystem contents differ.
A hardened container runs with a read-only root filesystem. Its application still needs a small writable location for temporary runtime files.
A production image includes compilers, build utilities and package caches. Only the built application and its runtime dependencies are required in production.
Small application edits cause dependency installation to rerun during every image build. The team is reviewing Dockerfile order and build inputs.
An image build needs temporary access to a private dependency registry. The credential must not become part of the distributed image artifact.
Two deployments using the same human-readable image tag run different builds. The release process needs a stable way to identify the approved content.
Two containers must communicate by service name on one Docker host. They are not expected to expose their internal ports publicly.
A Compose application starts a web service and a database. Database process startup takes less time than initialization needed to accept useful queries.
A container exits immediately when required configuration is missing. A restart policy starts it again, but the service never becomes usable.
The build system must publish images, while production hosts only need to retrieve them. Registry credentials are being reviewed according to those separate responsibilities.
A Docker host is nearly full. Some stopped containers and unused volumes may contain useful recovery data, so cleanup needs an inventory first.
A container is given access to the Docker daemon socket to inspect its neighbors. The security review must consider what operations that interface can authorize.
A developer wants to operate Docker without a root-running daemon. The design must account for rootless operation's networking, storage and privilege constraints.
A scan reports a serious vulnerability in a deployed image. The team must assess the finding and update the repeatable image release process.
A registry tag resembles an approved release but points to an unexpected image. The deployment process needs evidence of artifact origin and integrity.
A host kernel vulnerability affects machines running many containers. The team is determining which software layer needs remediation.
A new database application image performs a schema migration. Operators are considering reverting the image after the migration has completed.
ansible: An Ansible project manages staging and production machines. Before applying changes, the operator must establish which hosts the selected inventory and pattern resolve to.
A playbook contains tasks intended for different server roles. One operation must run only on web servers, so the play's execution scope needs review.
A repeated configuration run should maintain one intended line in a file. The current implementation uses a shell command that changes the file on every execution.
A team runs the same configuration automation twice with unchanged inputs. It wants to determine whether already-correct hosts remain stable on the second run.
A playbook performs ordinary application tasks and one package-installation operation. The controller's connection account is not root.
A role defines a default port, but one host receives a different value. Inventory and invocation-time variables are also present.
A fleet uses cached Ansible facts to choose operating-system-specific tasks. One machine has been rebuilt since its facts were last collected.
Several configuration tasks can change files used by the same service. The team wants a deliberate restart after relevant changes without redundant restarts.
An operator runs a playbook in check mode before production execution. Some later tasks depend on values returned by earlier commands.
A deployment reviews template changes using Ansible diff output. Some rendered configuration fields contain credentials visible to the job's log readers.
A project stores credentials with Ansible Vault and decrypts them during execution. A review examines what protection remains once tasks use those values.
Ansible renders a web-server configuration from variables. A successful render alone does not establish that the server will accept the result.
Several applications share an Ansible role. Its inputs and defaults must be clear enough that callers can upgrade it without relying on hidden assumptions.
A playbook works on a developer machine but cannot find a module on a clean CI runner. Collection dependencies must be reproducible.
Two installed Ansible collections contain modules with the same short name. The playbook must identify the intended implementation unambiguously.
A task should run only when a feature is enabled. The controlling value comes from an external input that may be a string rather than a boolean.
A later task uses the result of an earlier task. The earlier task can be skipped on some hosts, so not every run produces the same result fields.
A role includes tasks inside an outer loop, and the included tasks perform another loop. Variable names and per-item results must remain distinguishable.
A diagnostic command documents a nonzero exit code for a normal no-match condition. The playbook must distinguish that condition from an actual execution failure.
A read-only command currently reports changed and notifies a service restart. The team is reviewing how its result should be represented to Ansible.
A service runs across several hosts and cannot lose all replicas at once. A configuration rollout may restart each host's service.
A play targets application hosts, but one load-balancer operation must execute through a separate control host. Connection identity and variables must be checked.
A play uses serial batches and includes a database migration marked run_once. The migration must not execute repeatedly across batches or concurrent runs.
A deployment task fails after partially updating a host. The playbook includes a block and rescue sequence, and the resulting state must be understood.
A maintenance operation can take longer than a normal synchronous SSH wait. The team needs a bounded execution and completion-checking strategy.
Operators want to run only tasks tagged deploy. The full play normally prepares configuration and other prerequisites before reaching those tasks.
A cloud inventory plugin discovers hosts automatically. Staging and production share the account, so discovery filters affect the potential change scope.
A fleet-wide package installation uses many concurrent workers. A shared repository becomes overloaded before the target hosts finish.
A task handles a password with no_log enabled. It also writes a remote file, so output suppression and file permissions must be evaluated separately.
A playbook passes syntax validation and lint checks. It will reload a production service whose permissions, dependencies and runtime behavior need verification.
git: A developer edits tracked files and creates new files in a local Git checkout. Before committing, they need to inspect the current local changes.
One edited file contains two unrelated fixes. The developer wants the next commit to contain only one fix while keeping the other local.
A developer amends an existing commit after changing its message. They need to understand why the resulting commit identity differs from the previous one.
A developer creates a local feature branch and commits work on it. Teammates cannot yet see that branch in the shared remote repository.
The remote branch has new commits. A developer wants to inspect them before changing their current branch or working files.
Two feature branches modify related behavior. They have diverged, and Git can combine their files without a textual conflict.
A repository already contains a tracked credential file. A developer adds its path to .gitignore and needs to assess the existing exposure.
A developer has staged changes for a release commit. Some local debug configuration must remain outside that commit.
A developer rebases a branch that colleagues have already used as a base. The team must consider the consequences of publishing the rewritten history.
An incorrect change has reached a shared production branch. The team wants an auditable reversal without removing other people's published commits.
A developer wants to move a branch back one commit but has valuable uncommitted edits. They are considering the effects of reset modes before acting.
A release branch needs a specific hotfix from another branch that also contains unfinished features. The fix may depend on related changes.
Both sides of a merge changed the same security check. Resolving the conflict must preserve intended behavior, not merely remove conflict markers.
A local branch pointer was accidentally moved away from recent work. The developer is investigating which local records may still identify the previous commit.
A regression appeared somewhere among many recent commits. A reproducible test can distinguish an affected revision from a known-good one.
An agreed branch rewrite must be published to a shared remote. Another developer may have pushed since the last remote state was observed.
A pull request passes style checks but breaks a user workflow. The team is reviewing what its continuous integration checks actually establish.
A release passed staging tests, but production was rebuilt separately and behaves differently. The team is reviewing artifact identity across environments.
A CI workflow executes code submitted in pull requests by external contributors. The same project also has credentials capable of production deployment.
A workflow depends on a third-party action referenced by a mutable tag. An upstream change affects behavior without a change to the workflow file.
A build succeeds when a CI cache is present but fails on a clean runner. The cache key and undeclared build assumptions need investigation.
A production deployment awaits an approval decision. The team needs evidence that the intended artifact passed the required checks before releasing it.
A deployment changes both application code and database schema. Operators want to recover after a failure, but the schema change may not be reversible.
Two deployment jobs target the same environment concurrently. Their infrastructure and release changes can overlap.
A CI system uses federated workload identity to obtain cloud credentials. The trust policy currently accepts more repositories than should deploy this service.
A monorepo skips some tests based on changed file paths. A shared-library change affects applications outside the changed directory.
A release tag was moved after artifacts were published. The team needs to establish which source revision produced the downloadable release.
A test alternates between passing and failing on unchanged code. Repeated reruns are being used to obtain a green pipeline.
A release branch is meant to require a successful behavioral test before merge. A settings change may have made that test optional.
An organization receives a release binary but cannot establish its source revision or build workflow. The release process needs verifiable provenance.
observability: A team needs a dashboard showing how request volume and failure ratio change over time. It is choosing suitable telemetry for aggregated measurements.
An incident investigation needs the details of one failed operation among many successful requests. Records must carry enough context to locate that operation.
A user request crosses several services. The investigation needs the relationship and timing of the work performed for that request.
A service exposes a cumulative request counter. After a process restart, the raw value is lower than before, and the dashboard must handle that correctly.
A queue-depth measurement is sampled periodically. The queue can rise and fall between scrapes, so the team is reviewing what the measurement represents.
A latency SLO uses a specific duration threshold. The current histogram buckets are very wide around that threshold.
An application team proposes putting a unique request identifier in a metric label. The monitoring system already has limited series capacity.
Responders use a graph during an outage but cannot tell whether it shows a total, a rate or a percentage. The dashboard needs to support an operational decision.
Several service instances expose counters and can restart independently. A query must calculate the fleet's request rate without mishandling individual resets.
Two instances serve very different request volumes. Their dashboards show separate p99 values, and the team needs a percentile for the combined request population.
An error-rate alert stops firing when its target is no longer scraped. The team must distinguish healthy traffic from missing evidence.
Prometheus cannot scrape a target, but an external request test still succeeds. The investigation must separate telemetry collection from application availability.
Many dashboards repeatedly execute the same expensive expression. The team is evaluating precomputed metrics without changing the intended query meaning.
An alert fires on brief metric spikes that do not require intervention. The team needs to balance noise reduction against the required detection time.
One dependency outage triggers many related alerts. Responders need notifications that preserve useful context without creating a separate interruption for every symptom.
A host-down alert is accompanied by alerts from services on that host. The team is considering notification suppression rules tied to the parent condition.
A service samples only a small fraction of traces at request start. Rare failures are difficult to investigate because few affected traces are retained.
The tracing team wants to retain slow and failed requests preferentially. It is evaluating a policy that can use information available after spans have arrived.
A request enqueues work for another service. The worker's spans appear in a separate trace, and the team wants to recover the causal relationship.
A request has a useful trace and a detailed error log, but investigators cannot connect them reliably. Instrumentation fields are under review.
Trace attributes include HTTP headers that may contain credentials. The team must review collection and existing telemetry exposure.
An incident is discovered after the relevant telemetry has expired. Retention policy must reflect investigation needs and storage constraints.
An OpenTelemetry collector loses telemetry during peak load while applications continue running. Queues, retries and downstream capacity need inspection.
Production and staging emit indistinguishable telemetry for the same service name. The team needs consistent resource identity across signals.
Logs from a downstream service appear earlier than the upstream request that caused them. Distributed timestamps and causal identifiers both need consideration.
An API team is building its first user-impact dashboard. It wants a compact set of signals for request-driven service behavior.
A storage device shows moderate utilization but an increasing work queue. The team is choosing resource signals that explain contention and failures.
A homepage probe succeeds while checkout is broken. The team is reviewing whether synthetic monitoring represents the critical customer journey.
Detailed telemetry increases request latency at peak traffic. The team needs to preserve useful evidence while measuring and controlling instrumentation cost.
CPU and latency rise together after a release. Investigators must decide what additional evidence would support a causal explanation rather than a coincidental association.
kubernetes: A team submits a three-replica HTTP Deployment to a healthy cluster. The API accepts the manifest, but acceptance alone does not mean the application is ready.
A workload has an application container and a tightly coupled helper. The team is deciding whether they should share a Pod lifecycle.
A replicated API must change image version while continuing to serve traffic. Cluster capacity is limited, so temporary rollout capacity matters.
A database requires stable member identities and storage that survives individual Pod replacement. The team is selecting a workload controller.
A platform team needs logs from every eligible worker node, including nodes added after installation. Agent upgrades must also be controlled.
A reconciliation task runs every ten minutes and changes an external system. A run may be retried or overlap the next scheduled interval.
Several teams share a Kubernetes cluster and need distinct resource names, permissions and resource budgets. Some workloads have stronger isolation requirements.
An application deployment changes Pod labels while retaining an existing Service. Requests fail after the change.
A client connects to an internal Service address. The application listens on a different port inside its selected Pods.
An application can resolve public DNS names but fails to find a Service in another namespace. Network and DNS evidence must be separated.
Several HTTP applications need host/path routing through a shared external entry point. TLS certificates and the routing controller are managed separately.
A team wants to deny traffic by default while allowing DNS and a small set of application dependencies. The change must not take down existing critical paths.
An application has runtime settings that change independently of its image. It can receive configuration through environment variables or mounted files.
A database credential must be delivered to an application and rotated without unnecessary exposure or loss of service.
A worker needs to read one class of namespaced Kubernetes objects. Its API identity should not receive wider cluster administration access.
A user authentication succeeds, but a Pod API operation returns Forbidden. The team needs to inspect authorization rather than reset the login.
A latency-sensitive API shares nodes with other workloads. Measurements show variable demand, and the team must choose resource requests and limits.
A Pod remains Pending even though the cluster-wide resource dashboard shows unused capacity. Constraints may limit the nodes actually eligible for it.
A specialized node pool should serve a particular workload. The team must address both unwanted placements and whether the intended workload prefers or requires that pool.
An application needs a long startup interval, then may experience brief downstream failures while its process remains alive. Probe behavior must match those states.
A stateful Pod cannot start because its storage claim is Pending. The team must understand provisioning and placement before changing or deleting resources.
A cluster supports dynamic persistent storage through CSI. The team is tracing how a claim becomes usable storage for a scheduled Pod.
An API receives more traffic, but its HPA does not increase replicas. The bottleneck and metric availability have not yet been established.
A critical service runs several replicas across nodes. Planned maintenance must preserve useful capacity without making routine operations impossible.
A worker node requires maintenance while production workloads are serving traffic. Replacement capacity and eviction constraints need verification.
A container needs read access to configuration and write access to one data path. The team wants to reduce its privileges without breaking those requirements.
A deployment request fails before a Pod is created, and the API error references an admission webhook. The incident response must preserve the intended policy.
A release changes application code and its data schema. Errors appear after deployment, and rollback compatibility is uncertain.
Several replicas restart intermittently, but they do not all fail at the same time. The current container logs provide incomplete evidence.
A cluster disaster-recovery plan includes an etcd snapshot, but applications also depend on persistent data, credentials and external infrastructure.
